questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What does `volatile` do? When MUST you use it?
questions.source_text: What does `volatile` do? When MUST you use it?
questions.explanation: Tells the compiler: "every read/write must actually happen — no caching in registers, no reordering." Use it for: (a) variables shared with ISRs, (b) memory-mapped hardware registers, (c) variables changed by another CPU core or DMA.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: Can a variable be both `const` and `volatile`? Give an example.
questions.source_text: Can a variable be both `const` and `volatile`? Give an example.
questions.explanation:
Yes. `const volatile uint32_t *STATUS_REG = (uint32_t*)0x40020000;`
`const` = software must not write it. `volatile` = hardware changes it autonomously. Classic example: a read-only status register.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is `static` at file scope vs function scope?
questions.source_text: What is `static` at file scope vs function scope?
questions.explanation: File scope: limits visibility to this translation unit — the embedded equivalent of "private." Function scope: variable persists across function calls (stored in `.data`/`.bss`, not stack). Use for debounce counters, state machines.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: Why is `int` dangerous for embedded code? What should you use?
questions.source_text: Why is `int` dangerous for embedded code? What should you use?
questions.explanation: `int` size is implementation-defined (16 or 32 bits depending on platform/compiler). Use `<stdint.h>` types: `uint8_t`, `uint16_t`, `uint32_t`, `int32_t`. Never `int` in protocol code or hardware register access.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is undefined behavior? Give 3 examples.
questions.source_text: What is undefined behavior? Give 3 examples.
questions.explanation: (a) Signed integer overflow: `INT_MAX + 1`. (b) Shifting by width of type: `uint32_t x; x << 32`. (c) Dereferencing NULL or freed pointer. Also: reading uninitialized variable, out-of-bounds array access.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is the difference between `struct padding` and `packed` struct?
questions.source_text: What is the difference between `struct padding` and `packed` struct?
questions.explanation: Compiler inserts padding bytes to align members (e.g., `uint32_t` aligned to 4 bytes). `__attribute__((packed))` removes padding — useful for protocol frames but causes unaligned accesses which crash on strict-alignment CPUs or cause slow reads on ARM.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: `sizeof(struct S)` — will it be 5 for a struct with `char` + `int`? Why?
questions.source_text: `sizeof(struct S)` — will it be 5 for a struct with `char` + `int`? Why?
questions.explanation: Not 5 — it's 8 (on 32-bit). `char` at offset 0, 3 bytes padding, `int` at offset 4. Use `__attribute__((packed))` for 5 bytes, accepting unaligned access penalties.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is a `union`? Give a use case in embedded.
questions.source_text: What is a `union`? Give a use case in embedded.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is the difference between `++i` and `i++` in a for loop?
questions.source_text: What is the difference between `++i` and `i++` in a for loop?
questions.explanation: In `for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)` and `for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i)` — identical generated code. Difference only matters when the expression's value is used: `a = i++` (a gets old value) vs `a = ++i` (a gets new value).

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is type punning? Is it safe with unions in C?
questions.source_text: What is type punning? Is it safe with unions in C?
questions.explanation: Yes, in C11 (TC3) reading a union member different from the last written is defined. In C++, it is UB — use `memcpy` instead for C++.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is `restrict` keyword? Where is it useful in embedded?
questions.source_text: What is `restrict` keyword? Where is it useful in embedded?
questions.explanation: Tells the compiler: "this pointer is the only alias to this memory in this scope." Enables better optimization (no alias analysis needed). Common in `memcpy`-like functions. `void my_memcpy(uint8_t * restrict dst, const uint8_t * restrict src, size_t n)`.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: Why is `malloc` avoided in embedded production firmware?
questions.source_text: Why is `malloc` avoided in embedded production firmware?
questions.explanation: Non-deterministic time, fragmentation over time, no recovery from failure, heap size unknown at compile time, forbidden by MISRA/IEC 61508. Use static allocation: fixed-size buffers, memory pools.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is a memory leak? How do you detect it on a bare-metal MCU?
questions.source_text: What is a memory leak? How do you detect it on a bare-metal MCU?
questions.explanation: Track pool allocation counts (alloc_count - free_count). Stack painting (0xA5 pattern + watermark). Heap check functions in FreeRTOS (`xPortGetFreeHeapSize`). For Linux embedded: Valgrind, Valgrind massif, `/proc/self/status` VmRSS.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is stack overflow? How do FreeRTOS and bare-metal detect it?
questions.source_text: What is stack overflow? How do FreeRTOS and bare-metal detect it?
questions.explanation: FreeRTOS: stack painting + `uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark()`. Bare metal: fill stack with canary (0xA5A5A5A5), check at runtime. MPU: configure stack guard region (generates fault on overflow). Cortex-M: MSPLIM register (M33/M4 with TrustZone).

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: How do you implement a circular (ring) buffer?
questions.source_text: How do you implement a circular (ring) buffer?
questions.explanation: Head = write index (producer), tail = read index (consumer). Size must be power-of-2 for mask trick. Full: `(head+1) & MASK == tail`. Empty: `head == tail`. Lock-free for SPSC (single producer, single consumer).

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is endianness? Is ARM Cortex-M little or big endian by default?
questions.source_text: What is endianness? Is ARM Cortex-M little or big endian by default?
questions.explanation: Little-endian by default (can be configured BE8 in some variants, but virtually all real-world ARM embedded is LE). Network byte order is big-endian. Use `htons()`/`ntohl()` or manual `(buf[0]<<8)|buf[1]` for protocol parsing.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is bit-banding? What problem does it solve?
questions.source_text: What is bit-banding? What problem does it solve?
questions.explanation: Maps each bit in SRAM/peripheral to its own 32-bit word in a 32MB alias region. Enables atomic bit set/clear without read-modify-write (eliminates race condition with ISR). Available on Cortex-M3/M4. Not on M0/M0+.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is the difference between `uint8_t *p` and `const uint8_t *p`?
questions.source_text: What is the difference between `uint8_t *p` and `const uint8_t *p`?
questions.explanation: `uint8_t *p`: pointer to mutable uint8_t. `const uint8_t *p`: pointer to read-only uint8_t (can't write `*p`). For a const pointer: `uint8_t * const p`. For both const: `const uint8_t * const p`.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What does `__attribute__((packed))` do? What risks does it carry?
questions.source_text: What does `__attribute__((packed))` do? What risks does it carry?
questions.explanation: Removes struct padding. Risks: unaligned access — on Cortex-M0/M0+ this causes HardFault. On M3/M4 it works but slower (byte-by-byte loads). Pointer to packed member is not safe to dereference via unaligned pointer.

questions.category: 嵌入式 C/C++ 与内存
questions.title: What is the difference between `memcpy` and `memmove`?
questions.source_text: What is the difference between `memcpy` and `memmove`?
questions.explanation:
`memcpy`: source and destination must NOT overlap (UB if they do). `memmove`: handles overlapping regions correctly (uses intermediate buffer or copies in reverse). Use `memmove` when shifting data within a buffer.


## Section B — Interrupts and ISR

questions.title: List 5 things you must NEVER do inside an ISR.
questions.source_text: List 5 things you must NEVER do inside an ISR.
questions.explanation: (1) `printf` (uses heap, locks, blocking). (2) `malloc`/`free`. (3) `delay_ms()` or any blocking wait. (4) Lock a mutex (xSemaphoreTake — can block). (5) Floating-point without saving FPU context.

questions.title: What is a spurious interrupt?
questions.source_text: What is a spurious interrupt?
questions.explanation: An interrupt that fires with no apparent source (cleared flag, no pending source). Causes: electrical noise, race condition in flag clearing. Handle defensively: check flag in ISR, ignore if no source found, do NOT loop indefinitely.

questions.title: What does `volatile` fix in ISR-to-main communication?
questions.source_text: What does `volatile` fix in ISR-to-main communication?
questions.explanation: Without volatile, compiler may cache the flag in a register across loop iterations and never re-read from memory. Main loop sees stale value forever. `volatile` forces every read to go to memory.

questions.title: On ARM Cortex-M4, which registers are saved automatically on interrupt entry?
questions.source_text: On ARM Cortex-M4, which registers are saved automatically on interrupt entry?
questions.explanation: Hardware pushes 8 registers to stack: R0, R1, R2, R3, R12, LR, PC, xPSR. You must manually save/restore R4-R11 (callee-saved) if ISR uses them (compiler does this automatically for ISR functions via the EXC_RETURN mechanism).

questions.title: What is tail-chaining? Why is it efficient?
questions.source_text: What is tail-chaining? Why is it efficient?
questions.explanation: When an interrupt occurs while the CPU is handling another IRQ of lower priority, it chains directly without unstacking/restacking. Saves ~12 cycles. Effective when multiple IRQs are pending.

questions.title: What is preemption in the context of interrupts?
questions.source_text: What is preemption in the context of interrupts?
questions.explanation: A higher-priority IRQ can interrupt (preempt) a lower-priority ISR currently executing. On Cortex-M: configurable via NVIC priority levels. A pending IRQ preempts if its priority group > current active group.

questions.title: What is an NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt)? Give a use case.
questions.source_text: What is an NMI (Non-Maskable Interrupt)? Give a use case.
questions.explanation: Cannot be disabled by software. Always executes. Use cases: clock failure monitor, watchdog NMI mode, power-fail detection. On STM32: BXCAN errors can generate NMI, watchdog can be configured to trigger NMI.

questions.title: What is the NVIC? How do you set interrupt priority on Cortex-M?
questions.source_text: What is the NVIC? How do you set interrupt priority on Cortex-M?
questions.explanation: NVIC = Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (Cortex-M core peripheral). Set priority: `NVIC_SetPriority(IRQn, priority)`. Enable: `NVIC_EnableIRQ(IRQn)`. Lower number = higher priority. Number of bits implemented varies (typically 4 bits = 16 levels on STM32).

questions.title: What is the difference between interrupt priority and preemption priority?
questions.source_text: What is the difference between interrupt priority and preemption priority?
questions.explanation: STM32 uses group priority and sub-priority. Group priority determines preemption. Sub-priority breaks ties between same group-priority IRQs (no preemption, just ordering). Set via `NVIC_SetPriorityGrouping()`.

questions.title: Why must you clear the interrupt flag inside the ISR?
questions.source_text: Why must you clear the interrupt flag inside the ISR?
questions.explanation: If you don't clear the flag, the IRQ fires again immediately after returning → infinite ISR loop → system hang. Some peripherals clear on read of data register (UART RXNE cleared by reading DR). Others require explicit clear (TIM SR UIF cleared by `SR &= ~TIF_UIF`).

questions.title: What is lazy FPU context saving on Cortex-M4F?
questions.source_text: What is lazy FPU context saving on Cortex-M4F?
questions.explanation: By default, FPU registers (S0-S15, FPSCR) are NOT saved on interrupt entry to save cycles. Saving is deferred until the ISR actually uses FP instructions. If your ISR uses float: either set FPCCR.LSPEN=0 (eager), or don't use float in ISRs.

questions.title: What is priority inversion? What causes it?
questions.source_text: What is priority inversion? What causes it?
questions.explanation: High-priority task H blocks waiting for a resource held by low-priority task L. A medium-priority task M preempts L (M > L). H starves even though H > M > L. Solution: priority inheritance in mutex — L is temporarily elevated to H's priority.

questions.title: How does a binary semaphore differ from a mutex for ISR signaling?
questions.source_text: How does a binary semaphore differ from a mutex for ISR signaling?
questions.explanation: Binary semaphore: no ownership tracking, can be given from ISR. Mutex: tracks which task owns it (for priority inheritance). You CANNOT give a mutex from an ISR (corrupts ownership state). Use `xSemaphoreGiveFromISR()` with binary semaphore.

questions.title: What is a critical section? How is it implemented on bare metal?
questions.source_text: What is a critical section? How is it implemented on bare metal?
questions.explanation: Disable interrupts: `__disable_irq()`, access shared data, re-enable: `__enable_irq()`. On Cortex-M with priorities: use BASEPRI register to mask interrupts below a threshold without blocking NMI/HardFault.

questions.title: What is the difference between `__disable_irq()` and `BASEPRI`?
questions.source_text: What is the difference between `__disable_irq()` and `BASEPRI`?
questions.explanation:
`__disable_irq()` sets PRIMASK — disables ALL maskable interrupts. BASEPRI = N masks only interrupts with priority < N. BASEPRI is preferred in FreeRTOS (`taskENTER_CRITICAL()`) so NMI and HardFault still respond.


## Section C — Memory

questions.title: Draw the memory layout of a typical ARM Cortex-M application.
questions.source_text: Draw the memory layout of a typical ARM Cortex-M application.
questions.explanation:
```
0x00000000: Code (flash) — .text, .rodata
0x20000000: SRAM — .data (initialized), .bss (zeroed),
                   heap (grows up), stack (grows down)
0x40000000: Peripherals (memory-mapped registers)
0xE0000000: System (SysTick, NVIC, SCB, DWT, ITM)
```

questions.title: What is `.data` section? What is `.bss`? How are they initialized?
questions.source_text: What is `.data` section? What is `.bss`? How are they initialized?
questions.explanation: `.data`: initialized globals (e.g., `int x = 5`). Values are stored in flash at startup and copied to SRAM by the startup code (Reset_Handler). `.bss`: zero-initialized globals (e.g., `int y;`). Startup code writes zeros to this region. `.bss` is NOT stored in flash (saves flash space — only start address and size are needed).

questions.title: What is the heap? What is the stack? Where does each grow?
questions.source_text: What is the heap? What is the stack? Where does each grow?
questions.explanation: Heap: dynamic memory (malloc/free), grows upward from bottom of free RAM. Stack: function call frames, local variables, return addresses, grows downward from top of RAM. They grow toward each other — collision = silent corruption.

questions.title: What happens at stack overflow on bare metal?
questions.source_text: What happens at stack overflow on bare metal?
questions.explanation: Silent corruption. Stack grows into heap, .bss, or .data. Variables get overwritten with garbage. System may run normally for a while then crash randomly. No automatic protection unless MPU is configured with a stack guard region.

questions.title: What is a dangling pointer?
questions.source_text: What is a dangling pointer?
questions.explanation: A pointer that references memory that has been freed or gone out of scope. `int *p = malloc(4); free(p); *p = 5;` — UB. On bare metal: function returns address of local variable — stack frame gone, pointer points to garbage.

questions.title: What is use-after-free?
questions.source_text: What is use-after-free?
questions.explanation: Accessing memory after `free()`. Common bug: `free(p); if (p->flag) {...}`. The memory may have been reused by another allocation. Fix: `free(p); p = NULL;` — then NULL dereference is detectable.

questions.title: What is the difference between `NULL` and a wild (uninitialized) pointer?
questions.source_text: What is the difference between `NULL` and a wild (uninitialized) pointer?
questions.explanation: NULL: pointer value of 0, explicitly invalid. Dereferencing causes fault (if MPU/MMU enabled). Wild pointer: uninitialized pointer with random value — can point anywhere, dereference corrupts random memory. Always initialize pointers.

questions.title: What is memory fragmentation? Why does it matter in long-running systems?
questions.source_text: What is memory fragmentation? Why does it matter in long-running systems?
questions.explanation: After many alloc/free cycles, free memory exists in many small non-contiguous holes. A large allocation fails even though total free bytes > requested size. Embedded mitigation: fixed-size memory pools, allocate at startup only, never free.

questions.title: What is a memory pool? What are its advantages?
questions.source_text: What is a memory pool? What are its advantages?
questions.explanation: Pre-allocated array of N fixed-size blocks. `alloc()`: O(1), returns next free block. `free()`: marks block as available. No fragmentation (all blocks same size). Used in FreeRTOS queues, CAN message buffers, sensor data buffers.

questions.title: What is `__attribute__((section(".ccm")))` used for?
questions.source_text: What is `__attribute__((section(".ccm")))` used for?
questions.explanation: Places the variable in a named linker section. The linker script maps `.ccm` to Core-Coupled Memory (CCM SRAM) on STM32F4 (64 KB at 0x10000000). CCM is connected directly to CPU D-bus — fastest possible data access. DMA cannot access CCM.

questions.title: What is CCMRAM on STM32? What can you NOT do with it?
questions.source_text: What is CCMRAM on STM32? What can you NOT do with it?
questions.explanation: DMA cannot access CCMRAM. Only CPU can. Use for: fast lookup tables, stack, RTOS data. Don't put: DMA buffers, shared peripherals buffers.

questions.title: How does the startup code initialize `.data` and `.bss`?
questions.source_text: How does the startup code initialize `.data` and `.bss`?
questions.explanation:
Reset_Handler in startup_stm32xxxx.s:
1. Copy `.data` from flash (`_sidata` to `_edata`) to SRAM (`_sdata`).
2. Zero `.bss` from `_sbss` to `_ebss`.
3. Call `SystemInit()`.
4. Call `main()`.

questions.title: What is the linker script's role in embedded?
questions.source_text: What is the linker script's role in embedded?
questions.explanation: Defines memory regions (FLASH, RAM sizes and addresses), sections (.text, .data, .bss, .stack, .heap), and symbols (`_estack`, `_sidata`) used by startup code. Also places code in specific sections (`.ramfunc`, `.ccm`).

questions.title: What is SRAM1 vs SRAM2 on STM32? Why are they separate?
questions.source_text: What is SRAM1 vs SRAM2 on STM32? Why are they separate?
questions.explanation: SRAM1 (112 KB): general purpose, DMA accessible, slower. SRAM2 (16 KB): parity-protected on some variants. Both at 0x20000000 region but physically separate — matters for MPU region configuration.

questions.title: What is DMA? How does it avoid CPU involvement in data transfer?
questions.source_text: What is DMA? How does it avoid CPU involvement in data transfer?
questions.explanation:
Direct Memory Access controller moves data between peripherals and memory without CPU involvement. CPU sets up source, destination, count, and starts. DMA fires interrupt when done. Frees CPU for computation while data transfers in background.


## Section D — Peripherals and Protocols

questions.title: What is the difference between UART, SPI, and I2C?
questions.source_text: What is the difference between UART, SPI, and I2C?
questions.explanation: UART: async, 2 wires (TX/RX), point-to-point, up to ~10 Mbit/s. SPI: sync, 4+ wires (SCLK/MOSI/MISO/CS), full duplex, multi-slave with 1 CS per slave, up to 100+ Mbit/s. I2C: sync, 2 wires (SDA/SCL), half duplex, multi-master multi-slave via 7-bit address, open-drain, up to 3.4 Mbit/s.

questions.title: What is baud rate? Calculate BRR for 115200 baud on 84 MHz clock.
questions.source_text: What is baud rate? Calculate BRR for 115200 baud on 84 MHz clock.

questions.title: What is the difference between TXE and TC flags in USART?
questions.source_text: What is the difference between TXE and TC flags in USART?
questions.explanation: TXE (TX Empty): DR is empty, ready to write next byte. TC (Transmission Complete): all bits shifted out onto the line (shift register empty). Use TC for RS-485 direction control (must not deassert DE until TC).

questions.title: What are the 4 SPI modes? Which is most common?
questions.source_text: What are the 4 SPI modes? Which is most common?
questions.explanation: Mode 0 (CPOL=0,CPHA=0): idle low, sample rising. Mode 1 (CPOL=0,CPHA=1): idle low, sample falling. Mode 2 (CPOL=1,CPHA=0): idle high, sample falling. Mode 3 (CPOL=1,CPHA=1): idle high, sample rising. Mode 0 is most common.

questions.title: What is clock stretching in I2C?
questions.source_text: What is clock stretching in I2C?
questions.explanation: Slave holds SCL low to pause the transaction — gives slave time to prepare data. Master must support clock stretching (not poll/timeout on SCL). Needed when slave has slow processing (e.g., reading flash before responding).

questions.title: What is an I2C bus lockup? How do you recover?
questions.source_text: What is an I2C bus lockup? How do you recover?
questions.explanation: Slave started sending but was reset mid-byte — holds SDA low. Master sends 9 clock pulses: most slaves will release SDA after seeing clocks. If not: assert STOP condition, then hardware reset. Kernel: `i2c_recover_bus()`.

questions.title: What is the I2C ACK/NACK mechanism?
questions.source_text: What is the I2C ACK/NACK mechanism?
questions.explanation: After each byte, receiver pulls SDA low during 9th clock = ACK. If receiver releases SDA = NACK. Master sends NACK before the STOP on the last read byte to signal "no more data needed."

questions.title: What is PWM? Write the formula for duty cycle with ARR and CCR.
questions.source_text: What is PWM? Write the formula for duty cycle with ARR and CCR.
questions.explanation: `Duty% = CCRx / (ARR + 1) × 100`. Frequency = `FCLK / ((PSC+1) × (ARR+1))`.

questions.title: What is input capture mode on a timer?
questions.source_text: What is input capture mode on a timer?
questions.explanation: Timer captures the value of CNT register into CCRx when a specified edge occurs on the input pin. Used to measure pulse width, period, or frequency.

questions.title: What is ADC oversampling? When do you use it?
questions.source_text: What is ADC oversampling? When do you use it?
questions.explanation: Average N consecutive ADC readings to reduce noise and increase effective resolution. 4× oversampling → +1 bit resolution. 16× → +2 bits. Hardware oversampling on STM32: set OVSR and OSR bits in CFGR2.

questions.title: What is DMA double-buffering? Draw the pattern.
questions.source_text: What is DMA double-buffering? Draw the pattern.
questions.explanation: DMA alternates between two buffers: while filling buffer B, CPU processes buffer A. When DMA completes A, ISR signals CPU, DMA switches to fill A while CPU processes B. Continuous data with no gaps.

questions.title: What is RS-485? How does it differ from RS-232?
questions.source_text: What is RS-485? How does it differ from RS-232?
questions.explanation: RS-232: single-ended, ±12V, point-to-point, max ~15m. RS-485: differential pair (A/B), ±5V, multi-drop up to 32 nodes, 1200m at 100 kbps. RS-485 requires direction control (DE pin).

questions.title: What is Modbus RTU? What function code reads holding registers?
questions.source_text: What is Modbus RTU? What function code reads holding registers?
questions.explanation: FC=03 reads holding registers. Frame: `[ADDR][0x03][START_HI][START_LO][COUNT_HI][COUNT_LO][CRC_LO][CRC_HI]`.

questions.title: CRC-16/IBM — what is the polynomial? What is the initial value?
questions.source_text: CRC-16/IBM — what is the polynomial? What is the initial value?
questions.explanation: Polynomial: 0x8005 (normal) = 0xA001 (reflected). Init: 0xFFFF. Input/output reflected. Used by Modbus RTU, USB.

questions.title: What is a CAN frame? What is DLC?
questions.source_text: What is a CAN frame? What is DLC?
questions.explanation: DLC = Data Length Code (4 bits), 0–8. Specifies number of payload bytes. Classic CAN: max 8 bytes. CAN FD: up to 64 bytes.

questions.title: How does CAN arbitration work?
questions.source_text: How does CAN arbitration work?
questions.explanation: Non-destructive bitwise OR. All nodes transmit simultaneously. Dominant bit (0) overrides recessive (1). Node loses arbitration when it tries to send 1 but sees 0 on bus — stops transmitting and retries. Lower ID wins (more dominant bits in ID field).

questions.title: When does a CAN node go to Bus-Off?
questions.source_text: When does a CAN node go to Bus-Off?
questions.explanation: Transmit Error Counter (TEC) > 255. Node stops transmitting (bus-off). Recovery: wait 128 × 11 recessive bits, then re-enter error active state. Or application reset.

questions.title: What is CAN FD? What's the max payload?
questions.source_text: What is CAN FD? What's the max payload?
questions.explanation: Flexible Data-rate CAN. Two-phase frame: arbitration at classical speed (up to 1 Mbit/s), data phase at up to 8 Mbit/s. Payload up to 64 bytes. Requires CAN FD controller and transceiver.

questions.title: What is SOME/IP?
questions.source_text: What is SOME/IP?
questions.explanation: Scalable service-Oriented MiddlewarE over IP. Automotive middleware protocol (AUTOSAR). Runs over UDP/TCP. Used for service discovery and RPC in automotive Ethernet. Replaces CAN in high-bandwidth applications.

questions.title: What is the difference between GPIO push-pull and open-drain?
questions.source_text: What is the difference between GPIO push-pull and open-drain?
questions.explanation:
Push-pull: driver actively drives high AND low — fast, no pull-up needed. Open-drain: driver can only pull low; high state requires external pull-up resistor. I2C SDA/SCL must be open-drain (allows multiple masters/slaves to share the bus without short-circuit).


## Section E — RTOS

questions.title: What is the difference between a preemptive and cooperative RTOS?
questions.source_text: What is the difference between a preemptive and cooperative RTOS?
questions.explanation: Preemptive: scheduler can interrupt any task at any time when a higher-priority task becomes ready. Cooperative: tasks run until they voluntarily yield. Preemptive provides bounded latency; cooperative is simpler but one hung task stops everything.

questions.title: What is a tick? What does `configTICK_RATE_HZ` control?
questions.source_text: What is a tick? What does `configTICK_RATE_HZ` control?
questions.explanation: Periodic interrupt (SysTick) that drives the RTOS scheduler. `configTICK_RATE_HZ=1000` → 1 ms per tick. All `vTaskDelay()` and timeout values are in ticks. Higher rate = better resolution but more CPU overhead.

questions.title: `vTaskDelay(100)` vs `vTaskDelayUntil`. What is the difference?
questions.source_text: `vTaskDelay(100)` vs `vTaskDelayUntil`. What is the difference?
questions.explanation: `vTaskDelay(100)`: delay 100 ticks from NOW. `vTaskDelayUntil(&lastWake, 100)`: delay until 100 ticks from LAST WAKE. `vTaskDelayUntil` is for precise periodic tasks — it compensates for processing time so the period is exact.

questions.title: What is a task's stack? How do you size it?
questions.source_text: What is a task's stack? How do you size it?
questions.explanation: Each task has its own stack. Size in words (4 bytes each). Include: local variables, function call depth, interrupt context (64 bytes), string buffers. Measure with `uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark()`. Never less than `configMINIMAL_STACK_SIZE`. Add 20% margin.

questions.title: What does `uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark()` return?
questions.source_text: What does `uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark()` return?
questions.explanation: Returns minimum number of WORDS remaining since task started. Lower = closer to overflow. Return of 0 = overflow occurred. Check periodically in debug builds.

questions.title: What is a semaphore? What are the 3 types in FreeRTOS?
questions.source_text: What is a semaphore? What are the 3 types in FreeRTOS?
questions.explanation: (1) Binary semaphore: 0 or 1, for event signaling. (2) Counting semaphore: 0 to N, tracks multiple resources. (3) Mutex: binary + priority inheritance, for resource protection.

questions.title: Why can you NOT give a mutex from an ISR?
questions.source_text: Why can you NOT give a mutex from an ISR?
questions.explanation: Mutex tracks ownership for priority inheritance. `xSemaphoreGive()` checks and updates the owner task's priority. In ISR, there's no valid task context — accessing task control block from ISR corrupts RTOS internals. Use binary semaphore + `xSemaphoreGiveFromISR()`.

questions.title: What is deadlock? Give a two-task, two-mutex example.
questions.source_text: What is deadlock? Give a two-task, two-mutex example.
questions.explanation: Task A: takes M1, then waits for M2. Task B: takes M2, then waits for M1. Neither can proceed. Both block forever. Prevention: always acquire locks in the same global order.

questions.title: What is livelock? How does it differ from deadlock?
questions.source_text: What is livelock? How does it differ from deadlock?
questions.explanation: Deadlock: tasks are blocked, waiting forever (no progress). Livelock: tasks are NOT blocked — they keep running and changing state, but still make no overall progress (e.g., two tasks keep yielding to each other in a loop).

questions.title: What is a message queue in an RTOS?
questions.source_text: What is a message queue in an RTOS?
questions.explanation: FIFO buffer with built-in synchronization. `xQueueSend()` blocks if full. `xQueueReceive()` blocks if empty. Provides both data transfer and task synchronization. Can be used from ISR with `xQueueSendFromISR()`.

questions.title: What is `portMAX_DELAY`? What risk comes with using it?
questions.source_text: What is `portMAX_DELAY`? What risk comes with using it?
questions.explanation: Wait forever. Risk: if the event never comes (bug, deadlock), the task is stuck forever. In production, use finite timeouts and handle the timeout case (log error, reset peripheral, etc.).

questions.title: What is heap_4.c vs heap_1.c in FreeRTOS?
questions.source_text: What is heap_4.c vs heap_1.c in FreeRTOS?
questions.explanation:
heap_1.c: simplest — only allocates, never frees. No fragmentation. heap_4.c: first-fit with block merging — supports `free()`, merges adjacent free blocks. heap_5.c: heap_4 but across multiple discontinuous memory regions.


## Section F — Linux Embedded

questions.title: What is sysfs? Name 3 things you control through it.
questions.source_text: What is sysfs? Name 3 things you control through it.
questions.explanation: Virtual filesystem at `/sys` exposing kernel objects as files. Control: (1) GPIO direction/value (`/sys/class/gpio`), (2) LED brightness/trigger (`/sys/class/leds`), (3) CPU frequency governor (`/sys/devices/system/cpu`).

questions.title: How do you toggle a GPIO from a Linux userspace application?
questions.source_text: How do you toggle a GPIO from a Linux userspace application?
questions.explanation: Option A (sysfs): `echo 17 > /sys/class/gpio/export; echo out > /sys/class/gpio/gpio17/direction; echo 1 > /sys/class/gpio/gpio17/value`. Option B (libgpiod): `gpioset gpiochip0 17=1`. Libgpiod is the modern preferred approach.

questions.title: What is a kernel module? How do you insert/remove it?
questions.source_text: What is a kernel module? How do you insert/remove it?
questions.explanation: `insmod mydriver.ko`: load into kernel. `rmmod mydriver`: remove. `modprobe`: handles dependencies. `lsmod`: list loaded modules. `dmesg`: check kernel log for module messages.

questions.title: What is a device tree? What does it describe?
questions.source_text: What is a device tree? What does it describe?
questions.explanation: Hardware description file (DTS/DTB) that tells the Linux kernel what hardware exists and how it's connected (address, interrupts, clock sources, pin configuration). Replaces board-specific code. Loaded by bootloader, parsed by kernel at boot.

questions.title: What is systemd? How do you write a service unit file?
questions.source_text: What is systemd? How do you write a service unit file?
questions.explanation:
```ini
[Unit]
Description=My Sensor App
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/sensor-app
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```
`systemctl enable myapp.service` — start on boot.

questions.title: How do you debug a kernel crash (Oops)?
questions.source_text: How do you debug a kernel crash (Oops)?
questions.explanation: `dmesg | tail -50` — find the oops. Look for: PC (program counter), LR (link register), call stack. Use `addr2line -e vmlinux <address>` to find source line. Or `gdb vmlinux` with core dump.

questions.title: What is strace? Give a useful strace command for debugging an embedded app.
questions.source_text: What is strace? Give a useful strace command for debugging an embedded app.
questions.explanation: Traces system calls of a running process. `strace -p PID` — attach to running process. `strace -e open,read ./app` — trace specific syscalls. `strace -o log.txt ./app` — save to file. Useful: find which file fails to open, which socket call blocks.

questions.title: What is a character device? How does it differ from a block device?
questions.source_text: What is a character device? How does it differ from a block device?
questions.explanation: Character device (`/dev/ttyS0`, `/dev/i2c-0`): byte-stream, no buffering, accessed sequentially. Block device (`/dev/sda`, `/dev/mmcblk0`): fixed-size blocks, buffered, random access, supports filesystems.

questions.title: What is unit testing in embedded? What tool do you use?
questions.source_text: What is unit testing in embedded? What tool do you use?
questions.explanation: Test individual functions in isolation. Tools: Unity (C), CppUTest, cmocka. Mock hardware dependencies (GPIO, SPI) with stub functions. Run on host PC for speed. Separate HAL from business logic to enable mocking.

questions.category: 测试与嵌入式故障调试
questions.title: What is MC/DC coverage? Why is it required in DO-178C?
questions.source_text: What is MC/DC coverage? Why is it required in DO-178C?
questions.explanation: Modified Condition/Decision Coverage. Each boolean condition in a decision must independently affect the outcome. Required by DO-178C (avionics Level A). Example: `if (A && B)` — test A=T,B=T; A=T,B=F; A=F,B=T. Not just branch true/false.

questions.category: 测试与嵌入式故障调试
questions.title: What is a HIL (Hardware-in-the-Loop) test setup?
questions.source_text: What is a HIL (Hardware-in-the-Loop) test setup?
questions.explanation: Real ECU/firmware running, with its I/O connected to a simulation model that mimics the physical plant (engine, motor, sensors). Stimulus injected by test PC via CAN/analog signals. Used to test without physical hardware, validate timing, inject faults.

questions.category: 测试与嵌入式故障调试
questions.title: How do you find a stack overflow bug at runtime?
questions.source_text: How do you find a stack overflow bug at runtime?
questions.explanation: FreeRTOS: `uxTaskGetStackHighWaterMark()` < safety margin → alarm. Stack painting: fill with 0xA5 at startup, scan backwards for first non-0xA5. MPU: configure guard region below stack → HardFault on overflow → log PC.

questions.category: 测试与嵌入式故障调试
questions.title: What is Valgrind? Can you use it on embedded targets?
questions.source_text: What is Valgrind? Can you use it on embedded targets?
questions.explanation: Valgrind runs on x86 Linux only. For embedded: run logic-only code on host under Valgrind (requires HAL abstraction). For ARM Linux embedded (Raspberry Pi, iMX8): Valgrind is available and runs natively. Not for bare-metal MCUs.

questions.category: 测试与嵌入式故障调试
questions.title: What is ASAN (Address Sanitizer)?
questions.source_text: What is ASAN (Address Sanitizer)?
questions.explanation: Compiler instrumentation (`-fsanitize=address`) that detects: use-after-free, buffer overflow, use-after-return, double-free. Adds ~2× memory overhead and ~2× runtime overhead. Supported on ARM Linux. Not available on bare-metal without runtime support.

questions.category: 测试与嵌入式故障调试
questions.title: How do you debug a hard fault on ARM Cortex-M?
questions.source_text: How do you debug a hard fault on ARM Cortex-M?
questions.explanation:
1. In HardFault handler: read CFSR, HFSR, MMFAR, BFAR from SCB.
2. PC from stacked frame (MSP or PSP + 6th word) = faulting instruction.
3. Common causes: CFSR.BFARVALID + BFAR = bad memory address, CFSR.INVPC = invalid EXC_RETURN, CFSR.UNDEFINSTR = undefined instruction.
4. Use `addr2line -e firmware.elf <PC_value>` to find source line.

questions.category: 测试与嵌入式故障调试
questions.title: What is a JTAG debugger? What is SWD? How do they differ?
questions.source_text: What is a JTAG debugger? What is SWD? How do they differ?
questions.explanation: JTAG: 4-wire (TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO) + TRST optional. Industry standard, supports chain of devices, can test board connections (boundary scan). SWD (Serial Wire Debug): 2-wire (SWDCLK, SWDIO). ARM-specific, saves pins, same debug capability as JTAG for single device. Most embedded boards use SWD.

questions.category: 测试与嵌入式故障调试
questions.title: You deploy firmware and it works in the lab but crashes in the field.
questions.source_text: You deploy firmware and it works in the lab but crashes in the field.
questions.explanation: (1) **Timing/interrupt**: longer cable, slower sensor response, missed interrupt. Use oscilloscope. (2) **Power supply**: voltage sag under load, EMI from motors. Check with scope on VCC. (3) **Temperature**: component out of spec, crystal drift, MOSFET threshold shifts. Test at temperature extremes. (4) **Stack overflow**: more data in field (full log buffers, etc.). Check watermark. (5) **Race condition**: different traffic patterns expose rare concurrency bug. Add logging, increase tick for debug build.

questions.title: Bug 6 — CRC Byte Order
questions.source_text: Bug 6 — CRC Byte Order
questions.explanation:
```c
uint16_t crc = compute_crc16(payload, len);
frame[len]   = crc >> 8;       // high byte first
frame[len+1] = crc & 0xFF;     // low byte second
```

**What's wrong?**
Modbus RTU specifies CRC as LITTLE-ENDIAN (low byte first). This code sends big-endian. The receiver's CRC check will fail.

**Fix:** `frame[len] = crc & 0xFF; frame[len+1] = crc >> 8;`

questions.title: Bug 9 — Unaligned Access via Cast
questions.source_text: Bug 9 — Unaligned Access via Cast
questions.explanation:
```c
uint8_t frame[16];
// ...receive frame via UART...
uint16_t length = *(uint16_t*)(frame + 1);  // BUG: offset 1 is not 2-byte aligned
```

**What's wrong?**
On Cortex-M0/M0+: HardFault (strict alignment enforced). On M3/M4: works but compiler may generate 2 byte-reads instead of 1 halfword load (slower, potential tearing on non-atomic access).

**Fix:** `uint16_t length = (uint16_t)((uint16_t)frame[1] << 8) | frame[2];` (no alignment assumption).

questions.title: Bug 11 — Modbus Register Byte Order
questions.source_text: Bug 11 — Modbus Register Byte Order
questions.explanation:
```c
uint16_t register_val = 1500;  // RPM

response[3] = register_val & 0xFF;    // BUG: LSB first
response[4] = register_val >> 8;      // MSB second
```

**What's wrong?**
Modbus registers are BIG-ENDIAN (MSB first). This sends little-endian. The master reads `(0x05 << 8) | 0xDC = 0xDC05 = 56325` instead of `0x05DC = 1500`.

**Fix:** `response[3] = register_val >> 8; response[4] = register_val & 0xFF;`

questions.title: Bug 15 — Timer Overflow in Subtraction
questions.source_text: Bug 15 — Timer Overflow in Subtraction
questions.explanation:
```c
uint32_t start = TIM2->CNT;
do_something();  // takes ~50ms
uint32_t elapsed = TIM2->CNT - start;  // BUG when counter wraps
if (elapsed > TIMEOUT_TICKS) timeout();
```

**What's wrong?**
If the timer wraps (CNT overflows from 0xFFFFFFFF to 0), `TIM2->CNT - start` gives a huge number, falsely triggering timeout.

**Fix:** **Actually this is fine** if both are `uint32_t`. Unsigned subtraction wraps correctly: `(0x00000005 - 0xFFFFFFF0) = 0x00000015` (correct elapsed time). The key: BOTH must be the same unsigned type. If start is `int32_t`, it breaks.

questions.title: Bug 17 — Bit Manipulation: Forgot to Clear Before Set
questions.source_text: Bug 17 — Bit Manipulation: Forgot to Clear Before Set
questions.explanation:
```c
void set_gpio_mode(GPIO_TypeDef *gpio, uint8_t pin, uint8_t mode) {
    gpio->MODER |= (mode << (pin * 2));  // BUG: ORs without clearing first
}
```

**What's wrong?**
If the pin was previously in `AF` mode (0b10) and you try to set `OUTPUT` (0b01), you OR 0b01 into 0b10 = 0b11 (Analog mode). Always clear the field first.

**Fix:** `gpio->MODER = (gpio->MODER & ~(0b11u << (pin*2))) | ((uint32_t)mode << (pin*2));`
